text: Bessie Smith (April 15, 1892 – September 26, 1937) was an African-American blues singer widely renowned during the Jazz Age, nicknamed the "Empress of the Blues" and formerly known as the "Queen of the Blues," and recognized as the most popular female blues singer of the 1930s. Inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989, she is regarded as one of the greatest singers of her era and a major influence on fellow blues singers and jazz vocalists. Born in Chattanooga, Tennessee, according to the 1900 census, Smith was reported to be born in July 1892; her age of 16 appears in the 1910 census, and a birth date of April 15, 1894, is recorded in subsequent documents and observed by her family. Her parents, Laura and William Smith—William being a laborer and part-time Baptist preacher—died when she was young; by age nine, her mother and a brother had also passed, and her older sister Viola took charge of her and her siblings, preventing her from receiving an education. Due to her parents' deaths and poverty, Smith experienced a "wretched childhood" and, with her brother Andrew, busked on street corners for pennies, particularly in front of the White Elephant Saloon at Thirteenth and Elm streets. In 1904, her oldest brother Clarence left home to join a traveling troupe led by Moses Stokes; he returned in 1912 and arranged an audition for Bessie, who was hired as a dancer rather than a vocalist because Ma Rainey was already in the group. Contemporary accounts suggest Ma Rainey helped Smith develop a stage presence, and she later performed in chorus lines, becoming a major attraction on the Theater Owners Booking Association (T.O.B.A.) circuit. Around 1913, Smith began forming her own act at Atlanta's "81" Theater, and by 1920, she had built a reputation across the South and East Coast. The success of Mamie Smith’s 1923 recording of "Crazy Blues," which sold over 100,000 copies, revealed a new market for black music, prompting Smith to begin her recording career in 1923 with Columbia Records, signed by talent agent Frank Walker after he saw her perform years earlier. Her first recording session was on February 15, 1923, engineered by Dan Hornsby, and her first record, "Downhearted Blues" backed with "Gulf Coast Blues," was a hit; "Cemetery Blues," released on September 26, 1923, was the first issued under Columbia’s new "race records" series. As her popularity grew, Smith became a headliner on the T.O.B.A. circuit and rose to become its top attraction in the 1920s, becoming the highest-paid Black entertainer of her time and traveling in her own 72-foot-long railroad car. Columbia’s publicity department dubbed her "Queen of the Blues," and the national press later elevated the title to "Empress of the Blues." Her music emphasized independence, fearlessness, and sexual freedom, implicitly asserting that working-class women did not need to conform to societal expectations to be respected. Despite her success, she was dismissed by Black Swan Records for being too rough, as she reportedly stopped singing to spit, and both white and Black audiences considered her a "rough" woman. Smith had a strong contralto voice that recorded well acoustically and became even more powerful with electrical recording; her first electrical recording, "Cake Walking Babies [From Home]," was made on May 5, 1925. She benefited from radio broadcasting, including a late-night performance on WMC in Memphis in October 1923 after a white-only concert. Musicians like Danny Barker and Tommy Dorsey compared her presence to that of a preacher due to her ability to move audiences. She made 160 recordings for Columbia, often with top musicians such as Louis Armstrong, Coleman Hawkins, Fletcher Henderson, James P. Johnson, Joe Smith, and Charlie Green; several of her recordings, including "Alexander's Ragtime Band" in 1927, became among the best-selling records of their release years. Her career was cut short by the Great Depression and the rise of sound in film, which ended vaudeville; she continued touring and occasionally performed in clubs. In 1929, she appeared in the Broadway musical *Pansy*, which was a flop, with critics noting her as its only asset. In November 1929, she made her only film appearance in *St. Louis Blues*, based on W. C. Handy’s song, directed by Dudley Murphy and filmed in Astoria, Queens, where she sang with Fletcher Henderson’s orchestra, the Hall Johnson Choir, James P. Johnson, and a string section. In 1933, John Henry Hammond, who also mentored Billie Holiday, asked Smith to record four sides for Okeh (acquired by Columbia in 1925); he claimed to have found her working as a hostess at Art's Cafe on Ridge Avenue in Philadelphia, though she was not a hostess and not until the summer of 1936. The recordings, made on November 24, 1933, were her last and marked a shift toward swing-era performance, featuring musicians like Jack Teagarden, Frankie Newton, Chu Berry, Buck Washington, Bobby Johnson, and Billy Taylor, with Benny Goodman briefly audible in one track. Hammond was not satisfied with the results and preferred her return to her old blues sound. "Take Me for a Buggy Ride" and "Gimme a Pigfoot," both written by Wesley Wilson, were among her most popular recordings. On September 26, 1937, Smith was critically injured in a car crash on U.S. Route 61 between Memphis, Tennessee, and Clarksdale, Mississippi; her lover Richard Morgan was driving and misjudged the speed of a slow-moving truck, hitting it side-on at high speed, which caused the tailgate to shear off the wooden roof of her Packard. Smith, likely with her right arm or elbow out the window, took the full impact. The first person on the scene was Memphis surgeon Dr. Hugh Smith (no relation), who estimated she had lost about a half pint (240 mL) of blood and noted a major traumatic injury: her right arm was almost completely severed at the elbow. He stated that this injury alone did not cause her death; instead, she died from extensive and severe crush injuries to her right side. Henry Broughton, a fishing partner of Dr. Smith, helped move her to the shoulder of the road. Dr. Smith dressed her arm and asked Broughton to call an ambulance, but when he returned about 25 minutes later, Smith was in shock. With no ambulance arriving, Dr. Smith suggested taking her to Clarksdale in his car; during the journey, an oncoming car failed to slow and plowed into his car at full speed, sending it into Smith’s overturned Packard. The oncoming car ricocheted into the ditch, narrowly missing Broughton and Smith. The young couple in the speeding car sustained no life-threatening injuries. Two ambulances arrived—one from the black hospital, summoned by Broughton, and one from the white hospital, based on a report from the truck driver. Smith was taken to the G. T. Thomas Afro-American Hospital in Clarksdale, where her right arm was amputated, and she died that morning without regaining consciousness. After her death, a widely circulated but now discredited story emerged that she died because a whites-only hospital in Clarksdale refused to admit her; this account was given by John Hammond in a DownBeat article in November 1937 and formed the basis for Edward Albee’s 1959 play *The Death of Bessie Smith*. Dr. Hugh Smith told biographer Chris Albertson that no ambulance driver, or white driver, would have thought of taking a Black person to a white hospital. Smith’s funeral was held in Philadelphia a little over a week later, on October 4, 1937; her body was initially laid out at Upshur’s funeral home and later moved to the O. V. Catto Elks Lodge to accommodate an estimated 10,000 mourners, though contemporary newspapers reported about seven thousand attendees; fewer attended the burial at Mount Lawn Cemetery in Sharon Hill. Jack Gee, her husband from 1923, thwarted efforts to purchase a stone for her grave, once or twice pocketing money raised for it. Smith’s grave remained unmarked until a tombstone was erected on August 7, 1970, paid for by Janis Joplin and Juanita Green, who had done housework for Smith. Dory Previn wrote a song titled "Stone for Bessie Smith" for her album *Mythical Kings and Iguanas*. The Afro-American Hospital (now the Riverside Hotel) hosted the dedication of the fourth historical marker on the Mississippi Blues Trail. In 1923, Smith met Jack Gee in Philadelphia, whom she married on June 7, 1923, just as her first record was released. During the marriage, she became the highest-paid Black entertainer of her day, heading her own shows with up to 40 troupers and touring in her custom-built railroad car. In the 1920s and 1930s, African Americans had limited access to spaces for gathering, leading to the creation of establishments like Buffet Flats, which offered expensive food, free-flowing alcohol, and sex shows; Smith frequented these after concerts with friends, including drag queens and gay men, who viewed it as a safe haven. Her friends reported that people paid top dollar to see the sex shows, and she engaged in sexual activities with both men and women, including her longtime friend and lover Ruby Walker, before and during her relationship with Jack Gee. The marriage was stormy, with infidelity on both sides, including Smith’s numerous female lovers; Gee was impressed by her earnings but never adjusted to show business or her bisexuality, frequently leaving, which Smith used as an opportunity to have affairs, including with her musical director Fred Longshaw. When Gee discovered one of her affairs, he physically assaulted her, but she quickly retaliated and once retrieved his gun and shot at him. In 1929, when she learned of his affair with Gertrude Saunders, she ended the relationship, though neither sought a divorce. Smith later entered a common-law marriage with Richard Morgan, Lionel Hampton’s uncle, with whom she stayed until her death. Songs such as "Jail House Blues," "Work House Blues," "Prison Blues," "Sing Sing Prison Blues," and "Send Me to the 'Lectric Chair" addressed social issues like chain gangs, the convict lease system, and capital punishment, while "Poor Man's Blues" and "Washwoman's Blues" are considered early forms of African-American protest music. Her music highlighted a subculture within the African-American working class and incorporated commentary on poverty, intra-racial conflict, and female sexuality. Her lyrical sincerity and public behavior were not widely accepted as appropriate for African-American women, and her work was often dismissed as distasteful or unseemly rather than as a genuine representation of the African-American experience. Smith challenged elitist norms by encouraging working-class women to embrace drinking, partying, and sexual freedom as coping mechanisms, advocating for a broader vision of African-American womanhood beyond domesticity, piety, and conformity—emphasizing empowerment, happiness, independence, sassiness, and sexual freedom. Though she was a powerful voice for many minority groups and one of the most gifted blues performers of her time, the themes in her music were unacceptable at the time, leading many to believe her work was undeserving of serious recognition. Her lyrics are often speculated to have portrayed her sexuality, as seen in Ma Rainey’s "Prove it On Me," where she sings, "Went out last night with a crowd of my friends."

Bessie Smith's lyrics often addressed social issues such as poverty, intra-racial conflict, and female sexuality, and her lyrical sincerity and public behavior were not widely accepted as appropriate for African-American women, leading her work to be dismissed as distasteful or unseemly rather than recognized as an authentic portrayal of the African-American experience. Her music challenged elitist norms by empowering working-class women to embrace drinking, partying, and sexual freedom as ways to cope with daily stress and dissatisfaction, advocating for a broader vision of African-American womanhood that included independence, sassiness, and sexual autonomy beyond domesticity, piety, and conformity. Despite being a prominent and gifted blues performer of her time, her themes were considered unacceptable in her era, though they became more widely accepted in later decades. Her lyrics are frequently interpreted as reflecting her sexuality; in "Prove it On Me," Ma Rainey sings, "Went out last night with a crowd of my friends. They must've been women, 'cause I don't like no mens.. they say I do it, ain't nobody caught me. Sure got to prove it on me," and African American queer theorists and activists have viewed both Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith as "gender-bending" role models from the early 20th-century blues era. Three of Smith's recordings were inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1973 for their qualitative or historical significance. In 2002, her recording of "Downhearted Blues" was added to the National Recording Registry by the Library of Congress, which selects recordings that are culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant. The song was also included in the Recording Industry of America and National Endowment for the Arts' list of Songs of the Century in 2001 and in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 songs that shaped rock 'n' roll. The U.S. Postal Service honored her with a 29-cent commemorative stamp in 1994. In 2019, Time selected her for their 1923 cover in a series of 89 covers celebrating women from 1920 onward. Rolling Stone ranked her at No. 33 on their list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time in 2023. The 1948 short story "Blue Melody" by J. D. Salinger and the 1959 play The Death of Bessie Smith by Edward Albee are based on her life and death, though both distort factual details—Albee attributes her death to racist medical practitioners, a claim later debunked by her biographer. Dinah Washington and LaVern Baker released tribute albums to Smith in 1958, and Hoyt Axton Sings Bessie Smith, released on Exodus Records in 1965, features her songs performed by folk singer Hoyt Axton. The Band's song "Bessie Smith" first appeared on The Basement Tapes in 1975, though it likely dates from 1970 to 1971; musician Artie Traum recalls Rick Danko, the co-writer, singing a verse of "Going Down The Road to See Bessie" at Woodstock in 1969. Her song "See If I'll Care" was sampled by Indian Summer on their self-titled EP in 1993, receiving critical praise for contrasting the post-hardcore and emo elements of the album, with renewed popularity noted when the discography was reissued in 2019. A 1997 biography by Jackie Kay was reissued in February 2021 and featured as Book of the Week on BBC Radio 4, read in an abridged version by the author. In the 2015 HBO film Bessie, Queen Latifah portrays Smith, focusing on her life and sexuality, and the film received critical acclaim, winning four Primetime Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Television Movie. In the medical show New Amsterdam, season 2 episode 16, character Reynolds cites the myth that Smith was denied care at a white hospital and taken to a black hospital as inspiration for his treatment plans, though the show later corrected the fact that she had an unmarked grave and acknowledged her legacy in the blues. Each June, the Bessie Smith Cultural Center in Chattanooga hosts the Bessie Smith Strut as part of the Riverbend Festival. Technical flaws in most of her original gramophone recordings—such as inconsistent recording speeds that altered pitch and variations in the center hole of master discs—distorted her vocal phrasing, key, and tone, sometimes shifting pitch by as much as a semitone. These issues were addressed in the 70 LP complete recordings and especially in digitally remastered versions, with some critics noting that American Columbia Records CD releases are inferior to later transfers by John R. T. Davies of Frog Records. Throughout her career from 1923 to 1933, Smith recorded 156 tracks for Columbia Records and 4 for OKeh, making her complete works easily accessible, first released in the 1970s across five double albums: The World's Greatest Blues Singer (1970), Any Woman's Blues (1970), Empty Bed Blues (1971), The Empress (1971), and Nobody's Blues But Mine (1972), later reissued on LPs and CDs in the 1990s as The Complete Recordings (Vol. 1–5). First editions were released on 10" and 12" LPs. Antologies of her work were compiled, though there was no official national record chart in the U.S. until 1936; national chart positions are post-hoc estimates by music historian Joel Whitburn.
